rows.what the ink shows: Inside the parentheses is one short upright stroke, slightly inclined, with no upper and lower lobes of a 3. Both enclosing parentheses remain separate.
The isolated glyph after pour has an upright ascender crossed by a short horizontal bar, with a small lower continuation. It is a crossed t, unlike the uncrossed V-shaped nu in the integral below.

After the looped d, the next glyph descends to a pointed low vertex and rises in a slanted right arm ending in a short outward hook. There is no transverse bar or extra stem; the following parenthesis is separate.

The small cancelled subscript lies to the right of the long phi descender. An upper upright and short crossing stroke survive, but several heavy zigzag cancellation strokes cover the body and lower return, so they do not securely distinguish an f.

The word has a low initial series of joined strokes, a pronounced q descender, and a rising terminal ue tail. The pen stops before a clear gap to the following word; no additional ment sequence follows.

The final letter is a small open e form with an acute accent above it. The ink ends immediately after that accented e, with clear paper to its right; no second terminal e is present. The initial d loop and tall t also remain visible.

Despite the horizontal cancellation through its baseline, the initial tall loop, the f ascender, several separate i dots, and the later tall t with the short final ion group remain visible above the stroke.

The cancelled leading letter retains an upper loop, a long descending stem and a short lower turn. To its right is a smaller star made from intersecting short strokes, below the top loop of f; the diagonal deletion strokes pass across both without removing those features.

An initial s-like turn, a low p stroke and a joined rounded group survive on the left. Two long cancelling strokes merge with the rest of the word, leaving isolated ascenders but obscuring the internal letters and final ending needed to establish spectralement.

At the left end of the cancelled line, the first letter has a tall curved upper portion and a lower rightward turn. A separate short i stroke and dot follow it before the next word. The cancelling line crosses their feet but leaves these features visible.

The proposed E occupies the small rounded group after Si. Its upper loop and low rightward continuation survive, but the middle and lower portions coincide with the thick cancellation, preventing a secure three-part E reading or a different segmentation.

In the proposed est un group, a short upper bar, a sloping hooked stroke and a later upright remain above or below the cancelling line. The connections and low letter bodies are merged into the deletion, so neither the s/t division nor both letters of un can be recovered securely.

The right-hand residue is covered by parallel heavy horizontal strokes and a long enclosing return. Only a few upper humps and tiny lower remnants survive; they do not provide a recoverable word sequence.

The upper slant and left vertex of a less-than shape are visible. Its entire lower portion is a dense retraced black block, with no clean white gap to determine whether a separate equality bar lies below the lower arm.

The deleted expression retains a broad phi loop, its long downward stem, and separate parentheses around the crossed t. The paper immediately below and to the right of the phi stem is clear: there is no separate small f stem or crossbar there. The diagonal and horizontal deletion strokes run through the main glyph and argument.

The cancelled text under the inserted right-hand limit has a few visible dots, short ascenders and a terminal rightward fragment. A thick horizontal deletion covers the x-height and connections of the phrase, so the complete word sequence continuité à droite cannot be established from the surviving ink.

The insertion begins with the large initial A-like turn and the compressed dotted ending of Ainsi, then the separated low on group. In identifie the d loop, crossed t, tall f stroke and following i dot stand above the low connected letters; the final e tail is distinct from the curved insertion underline.

The deleted line begins with a tall f-like stroke crossing the cancellation, followed by a short curved group and a later descending loop. The rising deletion stroke and the line above merge the middle letters; I cannot securely separate the whole proposed 'f et g étant'.

After the first cancelled group, short humps and a tall crossed stroke survive above a long black cancellation, with a final descending stroke before the closing parenthesis. The lower bodies and word boundaries are covered, so no recoverable five-word sequence is secure.

An initial dotted i survives at the left of the deletion; a tall medial stem and a second dot remain above the strike, and the q-like descender plus a short terminal upturn remain below/right. These surviving positions support 'implique' despite the cancelled connecting letters.

The two phi heads and their long stems remain at the ends, with an f-like low crossed stroke at the left and a hooked g descender at the right. A slant at the central relation survives, but the two cancellation bars run exactly through its lower strokes, preventing a secure choice between less-than and less-than-or-equal.

The upper sloping arm and right-pointing vertex are clear. The lower half is a heavily retraced filled wedge, extending downward at the left; it does not preserve a white separation that would prove or exclude a second equality bar. The nearby lambda relation has a clearly separated lower bar, but this occurrence remains merged.
The first capital has two rising sides joined by a descending diagonal, and a separate small p sits below its right side, with a round shoulder and downward stem.

The second capital again has two tall sides and a diagonal connecting trough; the small lowered p is separately visible immediately before the opening parenthesis, with its loop above a short descender.

The deleted word has an initial m-like upright/hump and a later tall t-like stroke, but its intervening rounded letters lie directly under the long strike. The surviving tops do not establish all of 'monotone'.

Above the deleted word there is a separate compact insertion: an open initial c, a short r/o group, a dotted i, two low s-like turns and the ending with a tall t and trailing e. Its own baseline is above the cancellation.

The short deleted word after R+ preserves an initial loop and crossing pair, an i dot above the middle, then a tall t and a short final e-like hook. The two strike lines flatten parts of the body but leave the sequence 'existe' distinguishable.

On the first cancelled line, the beginning has a p-like descending stem and scattered tops but the body of 'positive' is crossed through. Farther right, the tall initial d, the high l of 'le', and the open c followed by low a/s turns in 'cas' remain above the cancellation and support 'dans le cas'.

Between the separate initial f and final g-expression, nearly all bodies are covered by the long cancellation. A dot, small rounded tops and a second roughly parallel low stroke remain, but they do not supply a secure sequence of four words.

At the end of the second cancelled line, a g has a visible closed low loop; immediately to its right the short horizontal equality trace is followed by two upright boundary strokes around a tall crossed f. The vertical bars belong to the mathematical absolute value in the single candidate.
After the cancelled absolute-value formula, three small letters remain above the line: a rounded open e, a tall t with a rightward cross/foot, and a final open c turn.

The upper oval/long descending stem supports phi, but the cancellation is superposed on a further low teardrop loop to the right. That low shape could include a crossed f/g-like subscript or part of the deletion gesture; I cannot certify the source's bare phi or add a definite index. On targeted repeat inspection, the lower-right closed loop and its upward return are visible separately from the main phi stem, as the peer notes; however, their upper connection meets the heavy diagonal overstroke. I do not find a secure uncancelled upper g head or an exclusion of a looped f, so the stronger g reading is not adopted by this reader.

The insertion has a closed phi head with a long stem. At its lower right is a narrow f-like tall stroke descending below the small alpha; the alpha's loop/crossing sits at that stroke's upper right. The final short curve is separated like a comma. This vertical arrangement resembles the same page's f-with-alpha-exponent, rather than a full alpha-parenthesis-f-parenthesis sequence.

The main measure sign has one long descending left stroke turning into a rising right arm and small terminal hook, the same narrow nu shape visible in the marginal integral; it lacks the additional body needed for mu. Its lowered index is heavily overwritten: a descending curved stem survives, but the upper psi arms cannot be separated securely.

Targeted reconciliation at 2026-11-19T22:44:21Z: peer agrees on M0102 uncertainty, M0113 as varphi_{f^alpha}, and M0114 as nu with uncertain psi index. Peer reads M0112 as varphi_g at medium confidence. Reinspection of the existing complete crop confirms the low closed loop, but this reader retains the original M0112 uncertainty because the upper junction remains superposed and does not distinguish g from a looped f/cancellation trace.
